title: Dos and Don'ts of Do Nows
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane describes his 'Do Now' routine -- five retrieval-practice questions on a half-sheet students complete in the first few minutes of class while he takes attendance and handles arrivals -- and argues the format is easy to misuse in two specific ways. His first rule, 'don't do too much,' warns against using the Do Now to launch new content, since the teacher's attention is split during those minutes and unclear directions derail a lesson before it starts; instead he reserves it for mixed retrieval practice of content students should already know well. His second rule, 'don't spend too much time,' caps the routine at roughly three minutes from entry to review, with only a brief pass over answers and no deep dive into misconceptions in the moment -- instead, if many students miss the same question, he circles back later with a targeted mini-whiteboard mini-lesson rather than re-teaching on the spot. He closes with a list of what the routine buys him: an easy-to-prep, fast, retrieval-focused, fluency-building, and confidence-building start to class.
points: Kane's two guardrails -- 'don't do too much' (never launch new content in a Do Now) and 'don't spend too much time' (three minutes flat, brief answer review) -- directly target the two most common ways teachers misuse the format.

His deferred-reteach strategy -- noting which question the class missed, then circling back later with a targeted mini-whiteboard drill using varied numbers -- avoids derailing the Do Now's pace while still addressing the misconception.

The routine deliberately keeps content at review level (not new material) precisely because Kane has minimal bandwidth to help students during the entry window when he's also taking attendance and managing arrivals.

Kane frames the Do Now's value beyond content coverage: it builds fluency on small persistent trip-points (like treating 'x' as '1x'), and builds early-class confidence by ensuring most students get several questions right before harder work begins.
quotes: I use a "Do Now" in each class I teach. It's something students do when they first walk in the door, without any directions from me.
The mistake a lot of people make is that they try to use a Do Now to launch their lesson, to get into the main topic of the class.
I aim for three minutes flat, from when students enter the room until we go over the questions.
In general I'm skeptical of the value of going over questions. If I want to address something, I circle back to it afterwards.
The goal is to keep students thinking, practicing the specific skill and mixing in some other problems so they can't go on autopilot.
It’s a great time for some retrieval practice. There’s a lot of math I want students to remember. Retrieval practice is key to long-term memory.
